name: Context Engineering - Anthropic SDK
scope: A person with INTERMEDIATE proficiency level in Context Engineering with Anthropic SDK as a competency should be able to design and structure clear, layered prompts using system, user, and assistant messages; manage context windows, tokenization, and truncation; fluently use the Anthropic SDK (Python/TypeScript-JS) to construct, send, and manage multi-turn messages, including tool/function calls and streaming responses; implement and troubleshoot RAG pipelines using embeddings, chunking, retrieval, and prompt injection mitigation; engineer prompts for structured outputs (JSON, markdown, code), multi-modal inputs, and robust style or locale handling; manage conversation state with summarization, rolling context, and explicit user or session variables; evaluate and optimize context for accuracy, cost, and latency using test harnesses, metrics, and A/B tests; encode safety, compliance, and escalation rules into prompts, and use SDK/configuration features for guardrails; integrate Anthropic SDK into backend services with separation of prompt templates, RAG, tools, and safety logic; monitor, log, and analyze prompt/context usage for errors and regressions; document and version prompts, templates, and context flows using Git and shared repositories; and collaborate with domain experts to maintain best practices, governance, and safe, reliable context engineering across teams and environments.
long_scope:
{"sections":[{"name":"Core Concepts of Context Engineering with Anthropic Models","scope_included":"- Understand the purpose and role of "context" in LLM applications: how instructions, examples, and reference data in the prompt directly bound model behavior and reliability.
- Distinguish clearly between different context elements: global instructions (system), user requests, assistant messages, tool definitions, tool results, and reference documents.
- Explain Anthropic model capabilities and limitations that shape context design (e.g., long context windows, reasoning strength, sensitivity to phrasing, hallucination risks, non-determinism).
- Reason about tokenization and context window limits: approximate token counts, how different content types (code, prose, JSON, HTML, PDFs) impact token usage, and the consequences of truncation.
- Understand how model hyperparameters (temperature, top_p, top_k, max_tokens, stop sequences) interact with context design and when to prefer configuration changes vs. prompt changes.
- Recognize common modes of LLM failure that context engineering needs to mitigate (hallucinations, ignoring instructions, over- or under-constrained responses, verbosity, brittle formats).
- Understand the difference between prompt engineering (wording) and context engineering (holistic design of all inputs, structure, retrieval, tools, state management).
- Know when the model context alone is sufficient vs. when to incorporate external knowledge (RAG, tools, databases, APIs).","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Anthropic SDK Fundamentals for Context Engineering","scope_included":"- Use the official Anthropic SDK (at least one of Python / TypeScript-JS) fluently to construct and send messages-based requests for a variety of use cases.
- Understand the structure of a Messages API call: model selection, system prompt, messages array, tools / tool_choice, temperature / max_tokens / metadata, safety or beta options.
- Construct multi-turn conversations programmatically, preserving relevant message history and trimming or summarizing when needed to stay within context limits.
- Implement streaming responses and incorporate them into applications while still adhering to context constraints (e.g., progressive rendering of long answers with precise instructions to the model).
- Properly encode structured content in messages (JSON, XML, markdown, code blocks) and know when to separate content into multiple messages vs. a single large message.
- Handle common SDK errors and edge cases that affect context (e.g., context-length exceeded, malformed tool definitions, invalid JSON in tool schemas, rate limits leading to retries that may duplicate context).
- Use SDK features related to tools (functions) and tool_choice to shape when and how the model calls tools vs. responds directly.
- Understand SDK versioning and feature flags/betas that may change how context is interpreted (e.g., new models, new system fields, thinking/beta options), and design prompts robust to such changes.
- Manage sensitive data in SDK usage: avoid logging raw prompts with PII or secrets, use redaction where necessary, and design context so sensitive data is minimized or isolated.","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Context Structuring and Prompt Design Patterns","scope_included":"- Design clear, layered system prompts that specify role, goals, constraints, style, safety/compliance requirements, and formatting expectations in a stable, reusable way.
- Differentiate and correctly use system vs. user vs. assistant messages to implement stable behavior (system for invariants, user for task-specific inputs, assistant for in-context examples or running state).
- Apply common prompt/pattern structures (e.g., instruction → context → task, or role → constraints → examples → input → output format) consistently across use cases.
- Construct robust instructions for structured outputs (e.g., JSON schemas, XML tags, markdown sections) and reinforce them in context via examples and explicit validation rules.
- Use in-context examples (few-shot learning) judiciously: choose representative examples, balance their token cost vs. benefit, and refresh or rotate examples over time.
- Design prompts to handle ambiguity: ask the model to request clarification when inputs are underspecified, and encode fallback behaviors and assumptions explicitly.
- Implement task decomposition in context (e.g., "First reason step-by-step in a scratchpad, then produce a clean final answer"), while being mindful of allowed features and safety policies.
- Structure prompts for code-oriented tasks (refactoring, debugging, generation) with clear separation of given code, constraints, and expected outputs (patches, explanations, tests).
- Engineer prompts for multilingual or locale-specific behavior, clearly specifying language, region, formatting for dates/numbers/currencies, and fallback behavior.
- Prevent prompt injection and instruction override by designing robust layering: clear system instructions about precedence, explicit handling of untrusted inputs, and separation of instructions from content.
- Use explicit style guidance (tone, verbosity, target audience, reading level) so that outputs are predictable, and understand when to trade off style complexity vs. robustness.","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Retrieval-Augmented Context and Grounding","scope_included":"- Understand the goals and anatomy of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) in the Anthropic ecosystem: embedding text, storing chunks, retrieving, and injecting into the prompt.
- Design chunking strategies for documents and knowledge bases with attention to semantic coherence, chunk size vs. recall, and metadata (titles, sections, timestamps, authors, source types).
- Use embedding models (Anthropic or external) appropriately: handle input size limits, normalize or index embeddings, and balance recall vs. precision in similarity search.
- Construct retrieval prompts that:
  - Clearly label and separate retrieved context from user input.
  - Indicate source types (e.g., "From internal policy", "From product docs", "From user manual"), with citations.
  - Instruct the model to only answer from retrieved context or to explicitly say "I don't know" when information is missing.
- Engineer context that supports grounded answers: include relevant excerpts, minimal but sufficient surrounding text, and strong instructions against hallucinating beyond sources.
- Implement simple ranking and filtering of retrieved documents (e.g., by score threshold, recency, document type) before including them in the prompt to manage context window and relevance.
- Design prompts to produce source-aware answers (e.g., footnotes, inline citations, or separate metadata sections referencing document IDs or URLs).
- Handle conflicts and ambiguity in retrieved data by instructing the model on tie-breaking rules, preference order (e.g., newest policy wins), and when to escalate or flag uncertainty.
- Integrate retrieval into multi-turn flows: reuse previous retrievals when still valid, trigger fresh retrieval when the user query shifts topic, and summarize accumulated evidence when context is crowded.
- Manage performance and cost trade-offs in RAG: limit the number and size of retrieved chunks, add pre-filters, and avoid redundant retrieval on minor follow-up questions.
- Mitigate prompt injection in retrieved content (e.g., untrusted user-generated text) via explicit system instructions, content delimitation (fences/markers), and rules about ignoring embedded instructions.","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Working with Tools, Functions, and External Systems","scope_included":"- Design tool (function) schemas in the Anthropic SDK that are:
  - Well-typed with clear parameter names, descriptions, and allowed values.
  - Constrained enough to prevent ambiguous calls.
  - Aligned with downstream system behavior and constraints.
- Decide which tasks should be handled purely in-context vs. delegated to tools (e.g., database queries, calling business APIs, performing calculations, fetching live data).
- Engineer system prompts that teach the model when to call a tool vs. respond directly, including examples that illustrate correct tool usage and edge cases.
- Handle tool call results safely in context:
  - Inject tool outputs into the prompt with clear delimiters, labels, and metadata.
  - Prevent tool output from acting as instructions unless intended.
  - Manage size of tool outputs via truncation, summarization, or pagination.
- Orchestrate multi-step tool workflows: use the model to plan, select tools, and interpret intermediate outputs, while keeping prompt structure clear and bounded.
- Integrate external knowledge systems (databases, search, CRMs, ticketing systems) via tools and represent their responses in a model-friendly, structured way.
- Ensure idempotence and safety of tool calls by designing prompts that discourage repeated/unsafe actions (e.g., deleting resources, making payments) and encourage confirmation patterns.
- Debug and refine tool-related prompts when the model makes incorrect or suboptimal tool choices (e.g., wrong parameters, mis-ordered steps) by adjusting descriptions, examples, and constraints.
- Design tool schemas and prompts to support multi-language or multi-tenant contexts (e.g., locale-specific tools, tenant IDs in parameters) and ensure users’ data is isolated in context.
- Balance autonomy vs. control: understand how far to let the model orchestrate interactions vs. orchestrate via application logic, and encode those boundaries in system prompts.","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Multi-Modal and Structured Output Context Engineering","scope_included":"- Include non-textual inputs (where supported) such as images or document attachments, and design text prompts that explain how the model should interpret them and combine them with textual context.
- Encode document structure (headings, tables, lists) in a way that the model can reliably use: e.g., markdown, simplified HTML, or explicit markers for sections / cells.
- Engineer contexts for structured outputs:
  - Define expected JSON or object schemas with fields, types, and constraints.
  - Provide examples demonstrating correct structure and edge cases.
  - Instruct the model to avoid extra commentary and only output the structure when requested.
- Implement output validation loops: detect malformed model outputs (invalid JSON, wrong types, missing fields) and use follow-up prompts to repair or reformat responses.
- Design prompts for hybrid outputs (summary + structured data + citations), clearly separating sections and indicating desired formats and ordering.
- Handle long or complex tables by prompting for selective summarization, column/row filtering, or chunked extraction instead of full-table reproduction when context is limited.
- Specify handling of binary or opaque attachments (e.g., large PDFs) in context: instruct the model on what tasks to prioritize (summarization, extraction, classification) and how to refer to the document.
- Engineer prompts for log, metric, or event-stream analysis that convert noisy semi-structured data into structured insights while keeping token usage manageable.","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Memory, State, and Conversation Management","scope_included":"- Manage multi-turn conversations by deciding which prior messages to keep verbatim, which to summarize, and which to drop, based on relevance and recency.
- Design summarization prompts that preserve important facts, user preferences, decisions, and open questions in a compact form while discarding irrelevant details.
- Implement rolling context techniques:
  - Maintain a running summary of the conversation.
  - Keep the last few turns verbatim for immediate detail.
  - Periodically refresh the summary when it grows too large or drifts.
- Encode persistent user preferences and profiles (e.g., expertise level, tone, known constraints) as separate context segments, updating them when the user changes their preferences.
- Separate long-lived global instructions (product policies, domain constraints) from per-session and per-request instructions to avoid duplication and context bloat.
- Design prompts that refer explicitly to state variables (e.g., `user_profile`, `conversation_summary`, `active_task`) instead of relying solely on natural-language references.
- Handle topic shifts: detect when the user changes topic and adjust which prior context is considered relevant or reset parts of the prompt accordingly.
- Manage cross-channel or cross-device continuity by representing conversation state in a portable data structure (e.g., a structured DB record with summaries and key facts) and regenerating prompts from it.
- Avoid hidden assumptions by explicitly encoding constraints carried from earlier turns (e.g., "we agreed to only use OSS libraries"), so the model continues to respect them even after summarization.
- Design prompts for multi-part workflows where different phases reuse earlier outputs (plans, drafts, analyses), deciding when to re-inject full outputs vs. summaries vs. references.","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Evaluation, Testing, and Iterative Optimization of Context","scope_included":"- Create evaluation datasets (golden sets) of representative prompts, inputs, and expected behaviors to test the effectiveness of context designs.
- Define evaluation criteria and metrics appropriate to the use case: factual accuracy, task completion, adherence to format, style consistency, latency, and token cost.
- Run manual spot-checks and structured reviews of model outputs to identify patterns of failure attributable to context design (e.g., ignored constraints, weak grounding, brittle examples).
- Design small-scale A/B tests comparing alternative system prompts, context layouts, and retrieval strategies, and choose winners based on quantitative and qualitative signals.
- Use deterministic or constrained settings (low temperature, fixed seeds where available) during evaluation to isolate the impact of context changes from randomness.
- Build simple regression test harnesses that rerun a fixed test suite whenever prompts or context logic change, and monitor for regressions in key outputs.
- Interpret metrics related to context size (average tokens per request/response, truncation rate) and correlate them with performance and cost to inform optimization decisions.
- Iterate on prompts systematically: apply controlled, small changes, track diffs, and record the effect on evaluation metrics rather than ad-hoc trial-and-error.
- Incorporate user feedback and production logs (appropriately scrubbed) into the evaluation loop, turning real failures into new test cases and prompt refinements.
- Recognize when context-engineering alone is insufficient to meet quality goals and escalate to architectural changes (better retrieval, more structured tools, or different models).","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Safety, Compliance, and Guardrails in Context","scope_included":"- Encode safety and compliance policies directly into system prompts in a clear, prioritized way (e.g., content to avoid, escalation rules, checks before acting on certain requests).
- Understand Anthropic’s safety-related capabilities and limitations and how they interact with context design (e.g., built-in safeguards vs. application-level guardrails).
- Design prompts that instruct the model to:
  - Refuse or redirect unsafe or prohibited requests.
  - Provide safe alternatives or educational explanations when declining.
  - Avoid giving sensitive instructions (e.g., self-harm, crime, dangerous content) even if the user attempts prompt injection.
- Combine prompt-based guardrails with external filters (keyword, classifier, rules engines) and clearly encode in context what should happen when unsafe patterns are detected.
- Engineer contexts for regulated domains (health, finance, legal) to:
  - Include disclaimers and clarify that outputs are not professional advice.
  - Encourage conservative behavior and escalation to humans.
  - Avoid making definitive diagnoses or legal decisions.
- Handle PII and confidential data responsibly in context:
  - Minimize inclusion of unnecessary identifiers.
  - Encourage anonymization in prompts where possible.
  - Avoid echoing back sensitive data unnecessarily in responses.
- Design safe behaviors around tools that can perform harmful actions (e.g., sending emails, modifying data), including confirmation patterns, dry-runs, and explicit safety checks in the prompt.
- Anticipate and mitigate prompt injection attempts where users or retrieved content try to override safety instructions, by reiterating safety priorities and clearly delimiting untrusted content.
- Construct escalation and fallback flows encoded in prompts (e.g., "If unsure or if the request seems risky, respond with this escalation template instead of guessing").","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Performance, Cost Optimization, and Reliability of Context","scope_included":"- Estimate and control token usage per request by:
  - Measuring typical token counts of system, messages, and retrieved/tool content.
  - Setting reasonable max_tokens for responses.
  - Reducing verbosity while preserving necessary instruction clarity.
- Optimize context length through:
  - Aggressive but safe summarization of prior turns and documents.
  - Pruning irrelevant examples and redundant instructions.
  - Compressing metadata and using IDs instead of repeating long names.
- Balance model selection vs. context complexity: choose lighter or cheaper models for simple tasks, and design contexts so tasks are routed appropriately.
- Use streaming responses to improve perceived latency and design prompts suited to streaming (e.g., early partial answers that can be refined or appended).
- Implement fallback strategies for transient failures (timeouts, rate limits, partial outputs) that maintain context integrity and avoid inconsistent states.
- Design contexts to be robust to minor SDK or model changes (e.g., rephrasing capabilities, small behavior shifts) by avoiding overfitting to quirky phrasings.
- Introduce caching strategies at the context level (e.g., caching summarizations, retrieval results, static system prompts) to reduce repetition and cost.
- Design prompts that encourage concise yet complete answers when necessary to manage cost, and verbose outputs only where they add value.
- Understand and mitigate failure modes under load (e.g., increased latency leading to retries and repeated context, race conditions in state updates) through careful orchestration and prompt design.
- Monitor performance metrics and iterate on context layouts that improve latency and cost without degrading quality significantly.","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Integration Patterns and Architectures for Context-Heavy Applications","scope_included":"- Understand common architectural patterns for Anthropic-powered apps: single-shot assistants, multi-step workflows, copilots embedded in products, RAG services, and tool-orchestrated agents.
- Integrate Anthropic SDK calls into backend services (e.g., REST/GraphQL endpoints, background jobs) with clear separation of concerns between application logic and context-construction logic.
- Represent prompts and context templates as first-class artifacts (e.g., separate config files, templates, or modules) rather than scattering strings throughout code.
- Design abstraction layers that:
  - Encapsulate model calls with well-defined request/response types.
  - Centrally manage system prompts, retrieval pipelines, and safety instructions.
  - Make it easy to swap models or adjust context without large code changes.
- Implement orchestration flows for multi-step reasoning tasks (e.g., analyze → plan → act → summarize) where each step has its own specialized prompt and context boundaries.
- Decide where to place business rules: in code vs. in context vs. in external systems, and encode that separation explicitly to avoid brittle prompt-driven business logic.
- Use queues or workflow engines for long-running or multi-stage LLM tasks, ensuring that context is persisted and reconstructed reliably across stages.
- Plan for multi-tenant and multi-environment deployments by isolating and parameterizing context (e.g., tenant-specific instructions, feature flags for prompts, environment-specific tools).
- Recognize architectural limits where context becomes too complex, and propose refactors (e.g., decomposing a monolithic assistant into specialized micro-assistants).","is_non_core_section":false},{"name":"Tooling and Environment Setup with Anthropic SDK","scope_included":"- Configure and manage Anthropic API keys securely across environments (dev/stage/prod), using environment variables and secret-management tools.
- Set up SDK clients with sensible defaults for timeouts, retries, logging, and observability hooks.
- Use language-appropriate patterns (dependency injection, singleton clients, connection pooling) to reuse SDK clients efficiently.
- Establish a project structure that cleanly separates:
  - Prompt templates and system messages.
  - Retrieval / RAG modules.
  - Tool definitions and orchestration logic.
  - Safety and compliance configuration.
- Integrate local development tools (e.g., REPLs, notebooks, playground-style UIs) to iterate on prompts and context structures quickly.
- Use configuration management (YAML/JSON/ENV) to parameterize models, temperature, max_tokens, and feature flags related to context behavior.
- Maintain SDK version consistency across services, plan for upgrades, and test context behavior after upgrading SDK or models.
- Set up test harnesses and CI tasks that run LLM-focused tests (mocked or real) to guard against regressions when context or prompt templates change.
- Implement logging patterns that capture enough detail about prompts and context usage for debugging while complying with privacy and security requirements (e.g., redaction or hashing of sensitive fields).","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Monitoring, Observability, and Analytics for Context Behavior","scope_included":"- Instrument Anthropic SDK usage to capture key metrics: request counts, error rates, latency distributions, token usage, and model mix.
- Log prompts and responses (with appropriate redaction/anonymization) in a structured way that supports querying by use case, model, user, and version of prompts.
- Build or use dashboards that track context-related metrics, such as average context length, truncation frequency, RAG retrieval hit rates, and proportion of tool calls vs. direct answers.
- Analyze logs to identify systematic context issues (e.g., frequent non-compliance with formatting, recurring hallucinations in specific domains, repeated failure to call certain tools).
- Implement alerting around abnormal patterns that may indicate context regressions (e.g., sudden spikes in errors for a particular prompt template or use case).
- Tag and version prompts, templates, and RAG pipelines in logs so that behavior can be correlated with specific context configurations.
- Conduct periodic reviews of production transcripts to:
  - Discover edge cases not covered by current context design.
  - Identify opportunities to simplify or clarify instructions.
  - Surface safety/compliance incidents that require prompt updates.
- Feed monitoring insights back into the context engineering lifecycle by creating new test cases, refining prompts, and adjusting retrieval and tooling strategies.","is_non_core_section":true},{"name":"Collaboration, Documentation, and Governance of Context","scope_included":"- Document key system prompts, templates, and context flows in a shared, accessible format, including their intent, structure, and known limitations.
- Use version control (e.g., Git) for prompts, context templates, and RAG configurations, treating them as code with branching, reviews, and change history.
- Establish naming conventions and folder structures for prompts and flows (e.g., by product area, use case, or persona) so teams can find and reuse them easily.
- Participate in or help define review processes for prompt/context changes (e.g., PR reviews that check for safety, clarity, and consistency with standards).
- Maintain changelogs that record why specific context changes were made and what impact they had in evaluation or production.
- Collaborate with domain experts (legal, compliance, product, support) to encode domain knowledge and policies into context accurately and maintain it over time.
- Share reusable patterns and building blocks (e.g., safety paragraphs, formatting instructions, RAG headers) across teams to reduce duplication and drift.
- Contribute to internal best-practices guides and playbooks about context engineering with Anthropic SDK, updating them as models and features evolve.
- Ensure that governance policies (e.g., around PII, logging, allowed use cases) are reflected in prompts, templates, and tool definitions, and are auditable.
- Mentor more junior engineers on fundamental context-engineering practices, code review for prompt changes, and careful production rollout of context updates.","is_non_core_section":true}]}
